title: Steve Jobs Keynote at WEBMANIA (1996)
speaker: Steve Jobs
content:
Good morning.
Welcome to uh Thank you.
Thank you very much for coming to Webmania.
We got this really great theater and uh we're going to try to tell you about some products we're incredibly excited about and uh see what you think of them.
We've got a whole day planned.
I know some of you can't stay for the whole day, but we're hoping most of you can.
We've got I think uh four more talks uh starting about a half an hour after this one ends.
So I'm going to go into a lot more detail a little bit later if you can stay.
Um we've changed our name, as some of you may have known, from Next Computer to Next Software.
We've been a software company for two years and we finally got around to changing the name.
Um and uh I am Steve Jobs, the chairman and CEO.
What we'd like to do today is uh introduce our Web Objects product family.
Uh this is I think one of the most significant product introductions we've ever had in our 10-year history.
And uh we've been working on this stuff in many ways literally for 10 years because approximately two-thirds of the product content is stuff that we have been perfecting over those years and has fit perfectly in the web.
And about a third of it is extending some of that to specifically address the web.
So these are very, very mature products hitting the ground very early on in the in the web's life cycle.
As we look at the web, everything that's been done to date, sort of from the beginning up till now, we sort of look at as Act One of the web.
And Act One has clearly focused uh on the browser.
Um we we have pages that get served over the web and and we can look at them miraculously from from anywhere on the internet with a web browser.
And what people have been doing with this is is what we call static publishing.
They have been looking at pages and navigating to other pages, but the quantum unit is a page.
And these pages need to have been made up by somebody, a person or several persons, using one of many tools you can do to construct these pages.
But once they're made, they're as they are until some human being changes them.
And so when you're looking at a page, there's probably 300,000 other people who could be looking at that same page.
It's not different for each person.
It doesn't change as the world changes until a human being gets in there and changes it.
And this very simple model has brought us a long way.
Here's an example of a static web page that some of you might have learned about Webmania from.
This is on our was our homepage until uh yesterday.
Uh here's another one.
Uh guy named Rick Smolan who did the a day in the life books is doing a day in the life of cyberspace on the web and he's published a website.
Uh here's Intel's homepage if you want to read about Pentiums.
Uh you can go there and and learn all about that stuff.
Here's another example of you know, educational one, a college.
Um here's one of my favorites.
And uh So you can go to just, you know, now hundreds of thousands of of of pages, probably millions by now and and uh see them just as everyone else can see them.
And this is very, very powerful and it's all focused on the browser.
Now, when you're consuming this information on the browser, um what you find is you want more.
And especially if you have a PC and you use the PC for other things, you find that the PC can do things that the web can't.
And that has to do with the user interface.
So let's say you're using Windows and um you like animation in Windows.
Well, you can't do that on the web today as an example.
Now, when you look at user interfaces, they all have capabilities.
They all have capabilities with limitations.
In the case of Windows, let's say that this square represents its user interface capabilities.
If that was the case, then proportionally, this is what a web browser can do user interface wise.
A small fraction of what you can do on Windows today.
And naturally, people want to enhance the user interface of the web browser so it can be more like their PC.
And that's been what's happening.
Most of what you read about in the news today concerning the web has to do with enhancing the user interface of the browser.
So as an example, we have plugins.
The Netscape browser has plugins and the most popular one is probably the the Macromedia Shockwave where you can download it and see some animation in your browser.
Play your director files in your browser just like you of course can on the PC.
Another big one we've heard about is Java.
Again, Java is an interpreted language that runs on the browser uh that will, you know, is is pretty close to being real out there and it will let you do some things like animations and run little applets to do things on the browser, primarily to enhance its user interface to try to make the surface area of that red square as close as possible to the surface area of the blue square.
And that's where most of the action has been in Act One of the web.
It has been to enhance the user interface.
Now, all that's well and good, but we're starting to move into Act Two of the web.
Because what people are finding is is that being limited to these static pages that people build by hand, they can't do some incredibly important stuff that they want to do on the web, especially if they're businesses.
And people want to now focus on the server, which is becoming the limit of what can be done and focus on how to provide what we call dynamic services instead of just static publishing on the web.
So again, the focus of Act Two is going to be on the server.
And what are what are the the essential issues on the server?
Let's take a look.
Let's go back to static publishing and kind of recreate that symbolically.
When you're going to do static publishing, you can think of it as taking a book or a brochure, in this case a brochure about Dodge cars and like tearing out or cutting out the pages very carefully and putting them on an HTTP server.
Now you probably recreate them another way, but metaphorically this is what you do and you could you could look at them all.
And this works great for some things, but what happens if the page that the customer wants doesn't exist?
What do you do then?
Now, how could that be?
How could it not exist?
Well, let me give you a few examples.
You can go to the Federal Express.
Matter of fact, how many people have used the Federal Express package tracking website?
Few.
Okay, let me explain it to those of you haven't seen it.
You go to the Federal Express's website, the www.fedex.com and you can get into package tracking.
And if you've just sent a package or if somebody's just sent one to you, you can type in the air the package tracking number and this application will go to, I believe it's four databases, find out where in the heck your package is and then it will need to build a web page to send back to you so you can see it.
How does it do that?
They they thought about hiring 10,000 gnomes to do this probably, but what they did instead was they have the computer build the web page dynamically.
It didn't exist one second and the next second it exists because the computer built it from all this data, sends it back to you and you can see exactly where your package is.
It's very cool.
We have over 10,000 people a day tracking their packages this way now.
Another example of course is is one of the many um web navigation products.
You want to type in, you know, web objects and find all the pages that on the web that have web objects.
You can use web crawler as an example.
It's a very good one.
Well, obviously your request needs to be answered in a custom way.
They're not going to have a web page with every answer for every question.
They'd have millions of web pages they'd have to build and they'd have to update them each day.
That's crazy.
So what they do is they take your request, they search their index database and then they build your response on the fly and send it back out to you.
Now, it turns out to do this, these are very, very trivial examples of dynamic services and yet they're very hard to build on the web today.
They take months and months and months to build.
So how can we make this a lot easier?
Well, this is precisely what Web Objects does.
Web Objects takes responses from customers, gets the information and dynamically builds web pages on the fly, hands them back to the HTTP server so that they can be served out to the customer making the request.
Where does it get the information to build those web pages?
It gets it from a library or a database not of pages, but of components to pages.
Pictures of cars, descriptions of cars, prices coming out of a flat file or SQL or some kind of a database.
It it gets the information from components and data sources to build these pages on the fly.
And what I'd like to do and oh and and in addition to that, there's a scripting language involved so that you can define how you want inputs from the customer treated.
You can define how all these components go together to build that page.
Let me give you a demonstration now of something we've built using this exact technology, which we call a virtual showroom.
We happen to use the Dodge car showroom as an example.
So let me show you what a dynamic website looks like.
Okay.
So I'm by the way using Windows 95 here and uh this is a Netscape browser running on Windows 95.
And what I've done is I've gone to the Dodge virtual showroom example site here that we have up on a server somewhere.
And what this allows me to do is this shows me all the cars that Dodge makes.
And so I'm going to select all of them for now.
And here's all the price points from $8,000 to $90,000.
And I'm going to select them all.
And here's all the models, two-door, four-door, van and truck.
I'm going to select them all.
And I'm going to sort by uh model type and I'm just going to say display cars.
Now, this information is going to be sent back to the HTTP server, which is going to pass it off to Web Objects, which is going to parse it all and it's going to look up in its database all this information and then sort it by model type, build a dynamic web page and send it back.
And here we go.
Here's the Avengers first because they begin with an A, the Caravans because they begin with a C.
And we can get down here.
There's a lot of Caravans.
Then there's Neons and then there's Ram trucks, right?
And then here's Vipers.
Okay, well let's go back and let's say I want to take all this information again and sort it by price and display the cars.
Well, obviously that's a completely different web page using the same data.
And so Web Objects is building that web page now and sending it back to me.
So now the Neons are at the at the front because they're the cheapest, you know, and here's uh here's a cheap Ram truck and the cheapest Avenger and you know, they're all kind of all mixed up just sorted by prices and probably if we go down here to the end, you know, we'll see that Viper.
There it is.
Okay?
Now, I'm going to go back up to the beginning.
Uh okay, and I'm going to pick Oh, come on.
There we go.
I'm going to pick that Neon.
Uh and uh let's take a look and see what we can learn about this Neon.
So we click on it and again, Web Objects builds this page on the fly.
And I can say, well, that's interesting.
I'd like to see what this car looks like in uh in, you know, in white.
So I'll click on the white paint chip.
Again, Web Objects is just going to go grab the white picture, rebuild the white page and send it out to me.
Or let's take a look at lime green.
Again, let's rebuild the page and send it back to me.
Now, you notice that we have op we have the base price of $9,500 here and we have options.
So I haven't picked any.
So let's go pick an option.
And again, these prices were gotten right out of out of the the uh the the database that's used to create this.
And let's pick package B. Uh and now what it's done is it's come back and built a page with a check mark on package B.
It's added it to the option price.
Somebody's done a calculation in the scripting language to add it to the option price and total it up.
Uh it's grayed out package 25B on the bottom because that's a subset I guess of package B.
Let me pick package package 25A too here.
And um so it'll build that web page and add it again with the total added.
And so now I've got a $14,000 car.
Let me go to leasing and um take a look at what we can do there.
What leasing's done is it's shoved the the total in.
I can put a down payment maybe of uh you know, $5,000 here.
Maybe I want to lease it over 60 months and I can say calculate it and it'll calculate my my lease payments.
So again, every one of these pages is being built on the fly because it it couldn't possibly be built beforehand.
There's too many permutations, too much data and too much input from the user.
So this is an example of a dynamic web page, of dynamic website built with Web Objects just like we saw that I I think is an order of magnitude more dynamic than anything on the web that we've seen today and it was built in about two days.
So that gives you an idea of the power of of Web Objects.
Now, we've gone even further than this.
The Web the Web Objects product and the and the virtual showroom I just showed you has some very sophisticated sort of flat file database technology in it if you will that you can use for this.
We have we decided to extend it to make three separate Web Objects products, each building on the one below it.
And so the second product in the Web Objects product family is Web Objects Pro.
Now, Web Objects via the scripting language allows you to connect the rich set of objects that come with Web Objects.
And it allows you to hook up to these flat file databases very in a in a very nice clean way.
But it does not allow you to add additional objects, which is something that if you're again going to build a even more sophisticated dynamic site, you may want to do.
And if you're going to add your own objects, you'll want to do it in a compiled language because the scripting languages while they're fast enough to connect objects together, they're not fast enough to really build objects with because they run in an interpreted mode versus a compiled mode.
So you need a compiled language and you can create your own objects and add them right into Web Objects and then connect them all together with the scripting language.
The third version of Web Objects goes even further and adds Next's extremely sophisticated enterprise database technology for connecting to very sophisticated enterprise databases and building very sophisticated applications using that data.
So we have three versions: Web Objects, Web Objects Pro and Web Objects Enterprise.
And this we believe, this kind of technology for building dynamic services is going to be the focal point of Act Two of the web in addition to Act One, which is enhancing the browser.
So let's take a deeper look at Web Objects.
We view Web Objects as something that can turbocharge any website and turn it from a static publishing website into a dynamic services website.
Web Objects works with all web browsers.
It is server-side software and it puts out standards over the web that work with any web browser.
Works with all HTTP servers.
Netscape's, any one of the public domain web servers, any web server.
It layers on top of any HTTP server.
Today it runs on Sun Solaris, Microsoft NT and Next Step and we have other versions coming soon.
Now, we talked about the languages, the need for a scripting language and the need for a compiled language in Web Objects Pro.
And after thinking very deep thoughts about the languages, we've decided to go with Java.
And so today we're announcing that we are going to be supporting both JavaScript from Netscape and Java in a compiled form uh originated in Sun fully.
And here's what we're doing.
JavaScript doesn't yet exist.
Uh the definition is not final and we are working closely with Netscape on that definition and we will have JavaScript as our scripting language as soon as it's ready, which we hope is going to be sometime uh this fall or early winter.
Compiled Java also doesn't exist.
The Java that we've all heard about is interpreted Java that runs on the cl on the browser.
But we for the server need compiled Java for the speed because if we're serving all these browsers, we have to run a lot faster than any single browser.
So we need compiled Java and again, we're working very closely with Sun on that and we will have that later on this year as well.
And so what we have done is today we have a very elegant script, a very simple scripting language called Web Script and as soon as we can get JavaScript, we are going to move to that, which we believe will be certainly by Q4 of '96.
And today when you write objects to move in to Web Objects Pro, the compiled language is C and we will move to compiled Java as fast as that is ready, working with Sun, which we also believe will be by Q4 of this year.
You can download beta versions of Web Objects today.
You can download the code and the virtual showroom demo also today.
And we want people to take that if you will as the example program for Web Objects and build your own virtual showroom out of it or cut and paste out of it to build whatever dynamic website you want.
And production versions are available the end of March.
Here's the website.
Uh you can simply choose your platform, Windows NT, Solaris or Next Step and be guided through a very simple download script.
Uh unfortunately, the traffic or I guess fortunately, the traffic at our website yesterday went through the roof.
Uh we maxed out our T1s.
There's been over a thousand downloads already and uh we are now moving the software out to alternate websites so that hopefully the traffic will be will be uh acceptable.
And so if you have a little trouble downloading it, try a few more times.
It'll it might take you a few minutes to get through, but but you will get through.
And we're doing everything we can to get a T3 as fast as possible.
Now, we've decided to take a new approach to pricing at Next.
Um We we have decided to give away uh Web Objects.
And uh this was a long and hard decision uh but we think it is the right one because we really believe that every website should have this software.
It is that good, it is that important.
And so uh when the production versions of Web Objects are ready, you'll be able to download them for free as well as the beta versions uh at the end of this month or end of this quarter right off our website.
Now, how are we going to make money on this?
Uh we we have thought of a way.
And here's the way.
Um the version of Web Objects that is free is the base version.
It's an incredibly powerful version.
We've often debated whether we're giving way too much away, but we've decided to go for it.
But we have the other two versions and the other the the base version has full dynamic services and the scripting language in it.
Web Objects Pro adds the ability to add custom objects.


---

## Part 2

with compiled code and we're going to charge $2,999 for that.
That also includes full support and also it includes full distributed objects.
So if you want to distribute your computational logics over several machines, you can do that with Web Objects Pro.
And the final high-end version for the enterprises, which includes our very sophisticated database technology, enterprise database technology is about $25,000 and up.
So we hope that Web Objects is going to really turn everyone on to dynamic websites and then a lot of people will buy Web Objects Pro and some in the enterprise will buy Web Objects Enterprise.

And again, what we believe is is that every website is going to go dynamic and every website needs Web Objects.
And so what we want to do by providing Web Objects for free is encourage everybody after they download their server from Netscape to go right to the next website and download Web Objects to layer on top of it and turbo charge that website free.
To help people get started, uh we have formed a consulting group called Web Architects and we do advanced website consulting.
We have over 40 consultants on board now.
We are one-stop shopping for advanced websites.
We will do consulting on technology all the way up to completely building websites for customers.
Uh creatively, artistically as well as the technology.
We are fluent in major enterprise issues, getting data off of main frames, etc.
We really understand this stuff because that's what we've been doing for the last many years.
We have six web engagements today with Fortune 50 companies.
So this is this group is up and running and we are doing some pretty sophisticated stuff and we are ready to help you.
If you have any needs, please get a hold of us.
We have, you know, people we can get available very quickly.

And now I'd like to focus on customers.
Uh our goal is to build a series of highly visible wins, both external websites and internal custom applications using web technology in large accounts to build our reference accounts base.
And we're pleased to announce that we already have several customers.
A lot of them won't let us talk about them at this stage uh for competitive advantage reasons, but four of them have graciously allowed us to uh discuss a little of what we're doing with them today.
Uh the first one is Mary Lynch.
Uh Mary Lynch is building major internal custom applications uh using Web Objects today.
And we have a whole team working with them and I think uh some of those applications may get rolled out to consumers uh during the course of 1996.
Another one that we can't say too much about is Motorola.
They are building major internal custom web applications again using Web Objects.

Next one is Dreamworks.
Dreamworks uh is building uh again some very sophisticated internal custom applications and they've chosen to build them on the web for the reasons that we have discussed, the multi-platform issues, etc.
And we're very pleased to have uh Dylan Kohler, who is in the Animation Technology division of Dreamworks up here with us today and what I'd like to do now is invite Dylan to come out and spend a few minutes telling us what they're doing with Web Objects.
Thank you, Dylan.

Thank you, Dylan.
Uh another customer that is a a long time customer of Next that has uh spawned a whole new area of relationship with us is Fannie May.
Uh we've been working with Fannie May for years.
Uh these guys are terrific.
As you know, uh Fannie May, if you will, coagulates home loans from the lending institutions, packages them up and sells them uh to the financial markets and has enabled millions of people to own homes that would not normally be able to.
In the process, they've become one of the most profitable corporations in the world.
And we're very pleased uh that Marty uh Colburn, the vice president of Technology integration could uh uh come out and be with us today from Washington DC and tell us uh for a few minutes what they are also doing with Web Objects.

Marty, thank you.

Thanks, Marty.
Thank you very much uh Marty and Dylan.
We've got other customers as well for this even though we're not yet shipping the products uh that we've been working with using the beta software and I think you're going to hear about a lot of them uh over the coming next few months.
What I'd like to do now is demonstrate Web Objects Enterprise for you uh and uh show you a real world application using um legacy enterprise data.
So what we're going to do again is use Web Objects Enterprise all the way up uh at the enterprise level into major uh corporate data in this case on a main frame in England.
And the company is OAG, the online airline guide.
I'm sure a lot of you've seen the book uh that looking up airline flights.
They have it on a CD ROM as well.
Uh they actually again get all of the airline flight information from all the airlines and then actually send it back out to the systems like Saber and the other airline reservation systems.
So they're kind of at the hub of this airline reservation uh wheel.
And they actually offer the ability to look up flights and book flights now uh on 3270 terminals.
Um and what they want to do is move that in you know, into this century from a UI point of view and move it on the web so that everybody has access to this and they have chosen Web Objects to do that.
So what I'd like to do now is is show you that demo.

So here we are.
Um let me go ahead and uh You can get the lights down on me so that's as visible as possible, please.
So let's take a look at this.
Um the first thing is it's going to ask me where I want to fly from and to.
So I'm going to say well we're near San Francisco, so it's it's going to pick all the airports going to the main frame database and picking all the airports.
I'll pick San Francisco International.
And um where I want to go, I'm going to say Chicago.
And I'll pick O'Hare and you see that it's rebuilt web pages now putting these things at the top, right?
So that's my my source and my destination.
Now what Web Objects has done is it's built a page and downloaded a Java applet onto that page and you're now seeing Java running on my Windows 95 with Netscape that was downloaded from Web Objects on a server somewhere over the net because of course Web Objects can download Java applets today on the browser.
Okay, um so let's go ahead and uh continue ordering my tickets here.
I probably have to pick now the day I want to fly and um so let's book it a little further ahead here so I can cancel this later on.
Uh February 29th, let's say.
And um I'm going to go ahead and maybe maybe take an evening flight here and again it's rebuilding the page with evening or maybe I'll go back to a morning flight.
Okay, and uh let's go ahead for flights now.
And it's going to go query the database and here's all the flights that fly from San Francisco to Chicago on Thursday February 29th uh in the morning.
And uh I'm going to pick maybe this one here leaving at 8:30.
I pick that one and uh hopefully it will come back and show me all the fairs.
Um I'm going to pick the cheapest one uh although I don't want to pick the one I can't cancel, so I'll pick this one here.
Um and so now it's confirming that flight.
Uh it's got my information here and I will say purchase the ticket.
So now it's it's going to to London to this main frame, so it might take a few minutes here, a few seconds.
And there we go.
There is my confirmation number.
I've actually booked this ticket now.
Every screen you saw was built on the fly based on my requesting more and more information or specifying more and more information.
Now, uh what I'd like to do now is we've got a phone hook up here.
Um could we get United Airlines on the phone, please?

Turn up the volume.
You can tell that this is real, can't you?

Hi, I would like to check a reservation, please.
I have a confirmation number.

Uh confirmation number is 6R1734.

Yeah.
Jobs, good job.
Mr. Jobs, uh-huh.

And what flight is that and what what day and where is it going?

I I don't have one.

And where's it going?

Thank you very much.

So again, I I hope that gives you a feel for the power of this.
Um and I hope you agree that that the website you just saw is orders of magnitude more dynamic than anything that exists on the web today.
Every single one of those pages could not have been pre-created because it was based on information I was putting in or information in the database.
If one of those flights was canceled, it would have been yanked and the page would have had to have changed.
There was no with with 10,000 gnomes, you couldn't build every permutation of pages that you would need.
They've got to be built on the fly.
And again, this app was complete this app's it's taken us about two weeks to write this.
Most of it frankly was interfacing with the main frame.
The actual app took only a few days to write with Web Objects.
So what I'd like to do now is is is ask you if you would to remember five things uh from today's presentation.
Uh the first one is that the second act of the web, the web act two is going to focus on the server because we have to now pay attention to the server to move from simple static publishing to really dynamic services like you just saw, which is what customers really want and which is what businesses really want so that they can provide information and services and products over the web.
So act two of the web is going to focus on the server.
Web second message is Web Objects works with all web browsers and all HTTP servers, including of course Netscape browsers and Netscape servers and we work very closely with Netscape to make sure that's all the case and we're all standards based.
So it works with all web browsers and all web servers.
Third, Java.
We are 100% behind JavaScript and compiled Java on the servers.
We are helping to enable those products to become real and we will have them as soon as anyone does on the server side.
And we believe that bringing those products to the server is going to be a major step forward.
Next, we are providing Web Objects for free.
Uh we believe this uh this is going to expose everyone to Web Objects and so there's no reason for not taking a look at this revolutionary new technology.
And lastly, we hope that it becomes a standard out in the marketplace and that everyone decides that they want to simply turbo charge their web server by coming to Next's website and downloading Web Objects for free on top of their web server and having the ability to now to create truly dynamic websites very, very easily.
And we hope that you're going to see our Web Objects powered by Web Objects logo popping up in a lot of websites in the next few months as people build websites even with the beta software, which is in quite good shape that you can download today and of course with the production software that you'll be able to download at the end of this quarter.
Now there are three additional presentations that will follow this one um by approximately uh I think 45 minutes or so and I'd encourage you to stay around to hear them.
Avi Tevanian, our vice president of engineering is going to take us through more technical details of Web Objects.
Jean-Marie Hulot uh is going to take us through in depth how simple Web Objects is to use and Chris Shoven is going to take us through really how to get started using Web Objects.
So I'd I'd encourage you uh even though it's uh raining today to to stay around for those other presentations.
Thank you very much for coming this morning.
Thanks.

## Part 1

(buzzing sound)
**[Steve Jobs]**: Good morning.
Welcome to uh Thank you.
Thank you very much for coming to Webmania.
We got this really great theater and uh we're going to try to tell you about some products we're incredibly excited about and uh see what you think of them.
We've got a whole day planned.
I know some of you can't stay for the whole day, but we're hoping most of you can.
We've got I think uh four more talks uh starting about a half an hour after this one ends.
So I'm going to go into a lot more detail a little bit later if you can stay.
Um we've changed our name, as some of you may have known, from Next Computer to Next Software.
We've been a software company for two years and we finally got around to changing the name.
Um and uh I am Steve Jobs, the chairman and CEO.
What we'd like to do today is uh introduce our Web Objects product family.
Uh this is I think one of the most significant product introductions we've ever had in our 10-year history.
And uh we've been working on this stuff in many ways literally for 10 years because approximately two-thirds of the product content is stuff that we have been perfecting over those years and has fit perfectly in the web.
And about a third of it is extending some of that to specifically address the web.
So these are very, very mature products hitting the ground very early on in the in the web's life cycle.
As we look at the web, everything that's been done to date, sort of from the beginning up till now, we sort of look at as Act One of the web.
And Act One has clearly focused uh on the browser.
Um we we have pages that get served over the web and and we can look at them miraculously from from anywhere on the internet with a web browser.
And what people have been doing with this is is what we call static publishing.
They have been looking at pages and navigating to other pages, but the quantum unit is a page.
And these pages need to have been made up by somebody, a person or several persons, using one of many tools you can do to construct these pages.
But once they're made, they're as they are until some human being changes them.
And so when you're looking at a page, there's probably 300,000 other people who could be looking at that same page.
It's not different for each person.
It doesn't change as the world changes until a human being gets in there and changes it.
And this very simple model has brought us a long way.
Here's an example of a static web page that some of you might have learned about Webmania from.
